title: Run a program
subtitle: What happens when I type ./hello?
why_it_matters: execve is the moment a shell stops being a parser and becomes a launcher. IR0 must resolve the path, read ELF, build a new address space, construct argv/envp/auxv, and iretq into ring 3 — then musl reaches main() without knowing it is not on Linux.

dual_view.kernel:
execve()
  ↓ resolve path (VFS)
  ↓ read ELF headers
  ↓ create mappings + stack
  ↓ argv / envp / auxv
  ↓ iretq → ring 3
  ↓ musl _start → main()

steps.label: Shell
steps.what_ir0_does: ash parses ./hello and calls execve. On success the shell image is replaced; on failure you see ENOENT or permission errors.
steps.why_it_matters: No fork required for simple exec — but job control often forks first.

steps.label: execve
steps.what_ir0_does: Syscall enters the process domain: validate path, load ELF PT_LOAD segments, setup stack with aux vector, preserve fd table per CLOEXEC rules.
steps.why_it_matters: Getting auxv wrong breaks ifunc, TLS, and ifunc-heavy libc.

steps.label: Resolve path
steps.what_ir0_does: Walk mount table from cwd to ./hello on MINIX (or tmpfs). Open inode, check execute permission.
steps.why_it_matters: Every exec is a filesystem walk first.

steps.label: Address space
steps.what_ir0_does: New mappings for text/data/bss/stack. CR3 loaded before user entry. NX and user bit enforced.
steps.why_it_matters: Exec is the heaviest MM operation in normal use.

steps.label: musl _start
steps.what_ir0_does: Dynamic or static entry sets up TLS, calls constructors, jumps to main.
steps.why_it_matters: libc is the real continuation of the kernel boot protocol for user programs.

steps.label: main()
steps.what_ir0_does: Your program runs. printf → write(1). Exit → exit_group → zombie until wait.
steps.why_it_matters: Everything above exists so this line can be boring.
